lines.note: Tsukaikuzushi means wearing out or exhausting through use or expenditure. The Portuguese begins Gaſtando, not OCR Gaitando; the abbreviated vſã- continues below.

runs.text: do deſtruir, ou conſumir de todo. Vt,

lines.note: Completes usando and explains total destruction or consumption through use. Taca- starts takara in the example on the next row.
Completes takara wo tsukai kuzusu, squandering wealth. The source separates tçucai from cuzzuſu, and deſba- begins the Portuguese continuation.
Completes desbaratar a fazenda, wasting an estate or property. The close printed ratara sequence is retained rather than silently respaced.
Tsukaiire concerns thoroughly training people in one's service. The printed ij sequence is retained, and gẽ- begins the abbreviated Portuguese gente.

runs.text: te, ou moços de que hum ſe ſerue. ¶

lines.note: Completes gente and includes servants or young attendants. Taca- now introduces a hawk as another object of training.

Completes taka wo tsukaiiruru, domesticating or training a hawk. The repeated i sequence corrects OCR tçucaſiruru; the Portuguese purpose continues below. The weak terminal punctuation is retained from the aligned reading.
The hawk is trained for hunting. The printed inſtruirlo and historical pera are retained rather than modernizing the attached object pronoun.
Tsukaisonzashi means mishandling or damaging a thing in use. Tratar is wholly italic, correcting the provisional roman T; da- continues danar.

runs.text: nar a couſa de que hum ſe ſerue.

lines.note: Completes danar and identifies the damaged thing as what one is using. The sentence finishes the misuse sense, not another entry.
Tsukaiushinai denotes wasting or spending away one's resources. Its caroned principal forms are retained as printed, with the Portuguese qualification below.
Completes gastar mal and illustrates wasting one's wealth. Zaifouo is retained without importing an accent from other occurrences; the example verb visibly ends in caroned ǒ.
Completes esperdiçar and reiterates squandering the estate. The close afazenda and the attached pronoun in gaſtala remain as printed.

runs.text: Retros, ou fio com que ſe

lines.note: Tsukamakiito is twisted silk or thread for wrapping a sword hilt. The historical noun Retros is retained without supplying an unestablished accent.
Specifies wrapping the katana's hilt. Catana is embedded in the Portuguese explanation; the historical emburulhão is retained.
Tsukamatsuri and its principal forms are glossed simply as doing or making. The brief Fazer does not specify the verb's full social usage, which is not added to the canonical text.
Tsukamaye means catching hold of something. The principal parts and the nasal abbreviation in algũa remain as printed.
Tsukami is grasping with nails or claws. The scan shows two f letters in Afferrar, correcting the provisional single-f spelling; the caroned past-form vowel is retained.

runs.text: como gauião, ou tigre, &c. Ou com as mãos.

lines.note: Hawks and tigers illustrate grasping with claws, followed by human hands. The historical gauião and the printed tilde carrier in mãos are preserved.

Zōhyō-domo refers to common soldiers, and ran no toki to a time of disorder. The example begins their grabbing things; both carons in Zǒfeǒdomo are retained without normalizing the historical spelling.

runs.text: Os ſoldados baixos no tempo da

lines.note: Completes tsukami toru, seizing or taking hold of things. The Portuguese begins its account of common soldiers acting during disorder.
Completes the example: during the upheaval the soldiers seize things. The Portuguese tilde-bearing forms are preserved occurrence by occurrence.
Tsukamiai denotes grappling or pulling at one another. Repeloẽs, including its unusual tilde position, is retained; the alternative explanation follows.

runs.text: contender afferrandohum no outro com as mãos,

lines.note: The opponents struggle while holding one another with their hands. The close afferrandohum sequence is retained rather than automatically divided into modern word spacing.
Adds grasping with the nails to the preceding account of grappling. This short row is a genuine continuation of tsukamiai.
Tsukamikoroshi means killing while gripping with the claws. Enlargement supports Tçucami- without the OCR's extra i after Tçu; the historical -oita principal part is retained.
Completes the explanation: kill by seizing with nails or claws. It describes the compound verb's action rather than supplying a separate example.
Tsukami idashi is pulling out after grasping. The final i in Tçucami corrects OCR Tçucaru, while the printed separation before idaxi is retained.

Completes tirar fora and gives zōfu wo tsukami idasu, grasping and pulling out the entrails. The faint tall type after Zǒ is read as f, replacing OCR Zǒ uuo; the damaged letter remains a nonblocking uncertainty. Af- continues below.

runs.text: ferrar das ẽtranhas, ou tripas, & tiralas fora.

lines.note: Restores the physical row omitted by OCR: grasp the entrails or intestines and pull them out. The abbreviation ẽtranhas is visibly printed with a tilde; ferrar completes Af- from c1-l029.
Tsukamitsuki means clinging by taking hold. This headword begins below the restored entrails sentence and retains its original stable ID.
Fune ni tsukamitsuku illustrates clinging to a boat. The Portuguese begins the manner of holding on, continued below.
Completes the example: grasp the vessel with one's hands. The printed mãos and embarcação retain their occurrence-specific diacritics.
Tsukamitori is taking by grasping. The upright principal parts and the italic Portuguese definition share this physical row.

runs.text: ſ. tomar por força, ou arrebatar.

lines.note: The continuation specifies taking by force or snatching away. The scan gives arrebatar, not OCR arrebalar; the explanatory abbreviation and indentation are retained.
Tsukanaga describes long sword hilts. The abbreviation cõpridos is retained, and Catana is embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
The example describes a long-hilted sword. Punhos corrects punhes; uppercase Catana in the translation is italic, while lowercase catana in the Japanese example is upright and not separately marked.
Completes cõ-pridos in the preceding translation. The brief fragment remains its own italic physical row rather than being merged upward.
Tsukane means gathering into bundles. The nasal abbreviation ẽ and the division mo-lhos are preserved rather than expanded or joined.
The example concerns bundling rice plants. The whole introductory Vt is italic, correcting the provisional split that left V upright.
Bate, ou arroz completes the rice example, then a paragraph sign introduces gathering the hair. Bate remains the printed historical noun; the Japanese example is upright.

runs.text: Ajuntar com amão os cabelos como madeixa,

lines.note: The translation describes gathering hair by hand like a lock or skein. The source's amão remains joined, and the explanation continues below.
The hair comparison ends with meada; te wo tsukanuru then introduces a posture of the hands. The long s and the abbreviation cõ are retained.

runs.text: as mãos hũa ſobre outra, ou com os dedos cru-

lines.note: The posture is one hand over the other or fingers crossed. The nasal hũa and the terminal division cru-zados are visible and retained.
Completes the crossed-fingers description as a sign of reverence. The historical reuerencia is retained, and no new entry begins here.
Tsukanoma is explained by zanji no aida, a brief interval. Breue corrects OCR Preue; the upright synonym after i, is not a typeface-term candidate.
The definition ends with an instant, followed by a very brief meeting example. The nasal abbreviation in taimẽ remains printed; its translation continues atop the next column.

runs.text: Viſta, ou encontro com alguem muito breue.

lines.note: Continues the preceding column's taimẽ example: a very brief visit or encounter. It is an indented italic translation, not a new headword.
Tsukanoma ni is the adverbial expression for a short interval. Adu. is italic apparatus, and the complete entry occupies one row.
The headword introduces incongruous or irrelevant things. The printed diſ- continues as ſonantes on the next physical row.
The example is saying something incongruous. The final yǔ has a caron, and the boundary between italic Vt and the upright Japanese example is retained.
Translates the preceding example as speaking these things. The two long-s forms and the short separate physical row are retained.
The adjective in -na receives the same meaning. Adject. and Idem. are italic; the faint mark after the stop is not additional lexical text.
Tsukarakashi means making tired. The example begins with upright V- for the horse word continued below; the paragraph sign does not belong to the headword.
Completes the example of making a horse tired. Caualo corrects OCR cauelo; its second a is weak, but the visible letter space and Japanese uma support this chosen reading.

runs.text: O ſegundo pouſo que fazem os paſ-

lines.note: This noun denotes the second landing of a bird flushed during hunting, distinct from fatigue below. The terminal paſ- begins passaros on the next row.

runs.text: ſaros aleuantados na caça como galinhas do ma-

lines.note: The hunting explanation includes wild fowl. The first fragment completes paſ-ſaros, and the final ma- belongs to mato; neither physical division is removed.

runs.text: to, &c. Poſto que algũa gente popular diga,

lines.note: The author adds that some ordinary speakers use a variant. Algũa retains its abbreviation, and the provisional Poſto rendering remains under the project's deferred st-ligature audit.
Tçucari is the upright variant cited by the preceding sentence, not an independent headword here. This standalone form is not marked merely for being Japanese.
This separate tsukare is fatigue or weakness. The final in- begins interior, distinguishing this definition from the bird-hunting sense above.
The definition contrasts inward fatigue with fatigue of the body. The short italic continuation completes interior rather than beginning a new word.
The verb means becoming tired or weak. The principal parts uru and eta and the two italic Portuguese alternatives remain as printed.
Tsukarefushi describes lying down from exhaustion. The worn headword agrees with the aligned reading; dei- starts the Portuguese verb continued below.
Completes deitarſe and gives exhaustion as the cause. The short row remains a continuation with both long-s letters preserved.

runs.text: O pedir com voz fraca, & ma-

lines.note: Tsukaregoi is a request made in a weak, plaintive voice. The ending ma- continues into the historical adjective mauioſa below.
The Japanese example is making such a plaintive request. The upright example lies between the italic end of mauioſa and the beginning of its translation.

runs.text: deſta maneira ainda que não ſeja pedinte pobre.

lines.note: This manner of asking need not be that of a poor beggar. The negative não is visible, and the complete translation remains one physical row.
This verb denotes entering or soaking in water. Dagoa is retained without inserting an apostrophe or modernizing its spelling.

runs.text: quente, ou fria, ou ẽ algũ rio, &c. ¶

lines.note: The definition includes hot or cold baths and rivers. The abbreviations ẽ and algũ are preserved, and the upright example begins with the printed Miz- division.
Mizzuni tçucaru means entering the water. The Portuguese is nagoa, not OCR nagõa; the fine diagonal crossing the region is a paper mark rather than a secure tilde.
This separate noun redirects the reader to Tçucare. Only Vide is italic; the cross-referenced headword is upright and not an embedded explanatory term.

runs.text: Cordão, ou cordel que poem ao derre-

lines.note: This homonym denotes a cord around a sack opening. Cordão and unaccented poem are retained; derre- continues as derredor below.

runs.text: dor nas bocas dos ſacos pera por elle como por

lines.note: The description places the cord at the sack mouths and compares its use with loops. The worn letter in bocas is b, and historical pera and elle remain.

runs.text: aſelhas puxarem algũa corda pera fechar, ou

lines.note: The loops permit drawing a cord through to close the sack. Aſelhas and abbreviated algũa agree with the scan; ou introduces the alternative below.
Adds opening the sack as the alternative to closing it. The short indented italic row completes the explanation without borrowing material from the next entry.
Tsukasa is a superior or chief. The headword's long s and the cedilla in cabeça are visible; this is a new flush-left entry.
Tsukasadori means ruling or governing. The principal parts are ru and otta; the divided ſenhorear and the upright letters do not require additional accents.
The example concerns governing a country. The Portuguese ends before italic Vt, followed by the upright Japanese verb divided at the printed hyphen.

runs.text: Ser ſenhor dalgum reino, ou gouernalo.

lines.note: The translation explains being lord of a kingdom or governing it. Ru completes the upright Japanese verb; dalgum and gouernalo retain their historical forms.

runs.text: ¶ Item, permet. Ser principal, ou preuale-

lines.note: The added figurative sense is being predominant. The joined abbreviation permet. is retained, and preuale- carries the verb into the next row.

runs.text: cer como nos humores que cauſão doença no

lines.note: The historical explanation illustrates predominance by humours causing disease. Humores has h, and cauſão and doença retain their visible nasal and cedilla marks.
The explanation ends with the body and medicines. Mezinhas corrects OCR mezinbas; the note records the dictionary's historical example, not a present-day medical claim.
Tsukaware is serving someone. The principal parts are ruru and eta; italic Vt introduces the separate upright example below.
Hito ni tsukawaruru is the example of serving a person. It is a complete upright sentence, not a Portuguese-embedded term or independent new entry.
Tsukawashi is sending, with an added sense of giving. The worn headword retains its aligned reading, and Itẽ preserves the printed abbreviation.
Completes the added sense of giving something. Algũa and the long s in couſa are retained in the short italic continuation.
The author prefers Xixa and gives Tçucaimono as a synonym. Meliùs is italic with a grave accent; the upright preferred form and synonym are not typeface-term candidates.

runs.text: Animaes dedicados aos Camis, em os

lines.note: Completes Tçucaimono, then describes animals dedicated to kami. Camis is a Japanese-derived term embedded in the italic Portuguese explanation and is marked for whole-word font review.

runs.text: quaes ellesſão adorados, & temidos por q̃ delles

lines.note: The sentence describes worship and fear of the deities in these animals. The close ellesſão and the abbreviation q̃ are retained rather than expanded or respaced.

runs.text: ſe ſeruem pera fazer mal, ou dar algũ caſtigo

lines.note: The historical account says the animals are used to harm or punish people. The abbreviation algũ and the long-s forms remain without adding a modern interpretation to the canonical text.

runs.text: aos homens, como minhoto de Atago, põba

lines.note: The examples include the bird associated with Atago and a dove continued below. Atago is an embedded name in italic, and põba is not silently expanded to pomba.
Fachiman completes the dove example. This historical spelling of the deity's name occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and is retained in italic for whole-word typeface review.
Tsukaye here means serving someone. The past form is eta, correcting OCR ota; the damaged final stop does not warrant extra text.
This homonym is a prop or support, and the headword reads Tçucaye rather than Tçueaye. Its example continues on the next page; the lower cayeuo is a separate catchword, not another body row.
